sections.h: Psalm 109: the longest curse, and Judas
sections.b: Psalm 109 has the longest string of curses in the Psalter (Psalm 109:6–19): a wicked judge and an accuser at the enemy's right hand, few days and another man in his post, begging children, a name erased in the next generation. The speaker is poor and falsely accused, and his own answer to his enemies is "I am all prayer" (Psalm 109:4). Two readings divide scholars: either he curses his chief enemy, or 109:6–19 quote the curse his accusers spoke against him. Peter applies Psalm 109:8, in its Greek form, to Judas, and the apostles choose Matthias to take his office (Acts 1:20–26). The psalm turns at "But you, LORD, my Lord" (Psalm 109:21) and sums up its hope in "They curse, and you bless" (Psalm 109:28). It is one of the three psalms left out of the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours.

common: Acts 1:20 applies Psalm 109:8 to Judas, and many Christians have read the whole psalm as a prophecy of the betrayer.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that Psalm 109:6–19 are the enemies' curse against the psalmist, quoted in his prayer, not his own words.

sections.b: Psalm 110:4 is the only place outside Genesis 14 that names Melchizedek: God swears to the king in Zion, "You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek." The king of David's line, ruling in Melchizedek's city, receives a priesthood older than Aaron's. The Talmud reads the verse as God's oath to Abraham, who took over the priesthood from Melchizedek (Bavli Nedarim 32b); the Qumran text 11QMelchizedek pictures him as a heavenly judge; Hebrews builds its whole teaching on Christ's priesthood on this verse, arguing from the oath, from "forever", and from Melchizedek's missing genealogy (Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 7:1–28). The Hebrew phrase 'al-divrati may mean "after the manner of" or "for the sake of", and some read malki-tsedeq as "a rightful king".

sections.h: Psalm 110: David's son and David's lord
sections.b: The New Testament quotes Psalm 110:1 more than any other Old Testament verse. Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son if David calls him "my lord" (Mark 12:35–37); before the high priest he joins the verse to Daniel 7:13 (Mark 14:62); Peter at Pentecost proclaims the risen Jesus seated at God's right hand (Acts 2:34–36). Jewish interpreters have read the psalm of Abraham (Rashi, following the Talmud), of David, or of a king of David's line, and point out that the Hebrew adoni, "my lord", is a title for a human being. Justin Martyr reports that the Jews of his day applied it to Hezekiah. Most critical scholars read it as a coronation oracle for a Judean king that later readers applied to the hoped-for king.

sections.h: Psalm 118: the rejected stone and the one who comes
sections.b: Psalm 118 gave the Gospels two of their key texts for Jesus' last week. The crowds greet him on the road into Jerusalem with "Hosanna" and "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name" (Psalm 118:25–26; Mark 11:9–10), and after the parable of the tenants he applies to himself the stone the builders threw out, which became the head of the corner (Psalm 118:22–23; Mark 12:10–11). Peter, Paul and 1 Peter make the rejected stone the cornerstone of the church (Acts 4:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8). The Targum reads the stone as the boy David, and Rashi as Israel among the nations.

sections.h: A king who is a priest
sections.b: Psalm 110:4 grants the king in Zion a priesthood "forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek", outside Aaron's line. Early kings did act as priests at times: David wore the linen ephod and offered sacrifices when the ark came to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:13–18), and Solomon blessed the people and offered at the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:62–64); but Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Hebrews uses the psalm to argue that Jesus, from Judah, is a priest of a different and permanent kind (Hebrews 7:11–25). Churches draw different conclusions about Christian ministers from it: see the card on Psalm 110.

The word frames the Hallel and its neighbors: it heads Psalms 111, 112 and 113 and closes 113, 115, 116 and 117. In 111 and 112 it stands outside the alphabet pattern, as a title. In Codex Vaticanus each closing Hallelujah of these psalms is moved to the start of the next psalm, so that there it comes only as a heading.

sections.h: The Hallel at the Passover meal
sections.b: The Mishnah has the Levites sing Psalms 113–118 while the Passover lambs were slaughtered, and has families sing them at the meal: the first part (Psalm 113, or 113–114) before eating and the rest after the last cup (Mishnah Pesachim 5:7; 10:6–7). The Passover Haggadah still does so. "When Israel went out from Egypt" (Psalm 114:1) gave the set its name, the Egyptian Hallel. If the Last Supper was a Passover meal, the hymn Jesus and his disciples sang before going to the Mount of Olives was the second half, ending with Psalm 118 (Mark 14:26; Matthew 26:30).

sections.h: The cup of rescue and the memorial of wonders
sections.b: Two verses in the Hallel group became part of Christian eucharistic prayer. "He has set up a memorial of his wonders ... He hands out food to those who fear him" (Psalm 111:4–5) was used by Thomas Aquinas in the office of Corpus Christi. "I will raise the cup of rescue and call on the LORD's name" (Psalm 116:13) was said by the priest in the Latin Mass before drinking from the chalice, and Paul's "cup of blessing" (1 Corinthians 10:16) uses the language of the Passover cups over which these psalms were sung.

sections.h: Psalm 118 at the Feast of Booths
sections.b: The Mishnah describes the priests at the Feast of Booths walking around the altar with willow branches each day, chanting Psalm 118:25, "LORD, please, save us now!", and seven times on the seventh day (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5). The seventh day came to be called Hoshana Rabbah, and the branches "hoshanas". Many scholars think Psalm 118 was written for this procession, with its gates, its festival offering and its branches up to the horns of the altar (Psalm 118:19–27). The crowds who wave branches and shout "Hosanna" at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem use the festival's words (John 12:13).

Psalm 115 answers the nations' taunt "So where is their God?" by mocking their idols: silver and gold, made by human hands, with mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands, feet and throats that do nothing (Psalm 115:4–7; repeated in Psalm 135:15–18). Its sharpest line is that "the ones who make them will end up like them" (Psalm 115:8): worship shapes the worshiper. 2 Kings 17:15 says the same of Israel, who "went after vapor and became vapor". Babylonian priests performed rites to "open the mouth" of a new statue; the psalm says the mouth stays shut.

Psalm 115:17 calls the world of the dead "the silent place" (dumah), and Psalm 116:3 speaks of "the straits of Sheol" closing in on a sick man. Like Psalm 6:5 and Psalm 88:10–12, Psalm 115 urges praise now, because the dead do not praise. Churches read the verse differently: as a picture of the grave before the fuller hope of resurrection, or, for Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses, as literal teaching that the dead are unconscious until they are raised (see the card on Psalm 115).

Psalms 111 and 112 are a matched pair. After a Hallelujah, each has 22 half-lines beginning with the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, eight verses of two lines and two of three. Psalm 111 praises God's works; Psalm 112 describes the person who fears him, using many of 111's words, so that the righteous person reflects God: "his righteousness stands for all time" is said of God (Psalm 111:3) and of him (Psalm 112:3, 9), and both are "gracious and compassionate" (Psalm 111:4; Psalm 112:4).

Book Five opens with Psalm 107, the thanks of those the LORD has gathered from the lands, which answers the plea that closes Book Four (Psalm 106:47). Then come David psalms (108–110): a new psalm made from 57 and 60, the curse psalm 109, and the royal oracle 110, the psalm most quoted in the New Testament. The twin alphabet psalms 111–112 lead into the Hallel (113–118), the festival set sung at Passover. From here the Greek numbering differs most: it joins 114 and 115 and splits 116 in two.

sections.h: The barren woman made a mother
sections.b: Psalm 113 praises the God who lifts the poor from the garbage heap, in words taken from Hannah's song (Psalm 113:7–8; 1 Samuel 2:8), and ends with Hannah's own story: "The barren woman of the house he seats as a glad mother of children" (Psalm 113:9). Isaiah later uses the same picture for ruined Zion (Isaiah 54:1), and Paul for the church (Galatians 4:27).

sections.h: An accuser at his right hand
sections.b: Psalm 109 uses the root satan, "accuse", four times for the singer's accusers in a court case (Psalm 109:4, 6, 20, 29). The KJV's "let Satan stand at his right hand" (Psalm 109:6, KJV) follows a long tradition, helped by the Greek diabolos, but the Hebrew has no article and most translations now read "an accuser", as at the high priest's right hand in Zechariah 3:1.

In Psalm 107:23–32 sailors are tossed to the heavens and the depths until "all their skill was swallowed up"; they cry to the LORD, and "he brought the gale down to a hush". Jonah's storm follows the same steps (Jonah 1:4–16), and the Gospels tell of Jesus rebuking the wind on the Sea of Galilee so that his disciples ask who he can be (Mark 4:35–41). In Psalm 114 the sea "saw and ran" at the exodus.
